title: Goldmann Applanation Tonometry (GAT): The Gold Standard in IOP Assessment
summary: Goldmann Applanation Tonometry remains the clinical gold standard for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP) by applying the Imbert-Fick Law. This guide covers the physical principles, standardized clinical application, and the diagnostic pitfalls every ophthalmic surgeon must master.

sections.title: Principle: The Imbert-Fick Law
sections.content: The Goldmann tonometer operates on the Imbert-Fick principle: For an ideal, dry, thin-walled sphere, the pressure (P) inside the sphere is equal to the force (F) required to flatten its surface divided by the area (A) of applanation (P = F/A). In GAT, the diameter of the circular flattened area is exactly 3.06 mm.

sections.title: Clinical Procedure (Step-by-Step)
content: 1. Instill topical anesthetic (proparacaine 0.5%) and fluorescein sodium.
2. Set the biprism to 10 mmHg as a starting point.
3. Position patient at slit-lamp with forehead firmly against the headrest.
4. Align the biprism with the central cornea under cobalt blue light.
5. Advance the probe until the semicircles meet.
6. Adjust the tension dial until the inner edges of the semicircles just touch.

sections.title: Red Flags: When NOT to Trust GAT
content: Excessive fluorescein: Causes overestimation of IOP.
Poor tear film: Leads to jagged, irregular, or missing semicircles.
Excessive eyelid pressure: Patient holding breath or blinking forces eye back (pseudoelevation).
Corneal scarring or edema: Distorts the applanation area, making 3.06mm diameter invalid.
Astigmatism > 3.00 D: Must align prism axis with -43° (minus cylinder axis) to avoid measurement error.

content.explanation: M: Measurement too early (too much force). I: Irregular semicircles. S: Squeezing (lid pressure). T: Thin/Thick corneal adjustment (CCT) ignored.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always disinfect the prism with 70% isopropyl alcohol and allow to air dry for 5-10 minutes to prevent transmission of adenovirus or prion diseases.
The standard 3.06 mm diameter exists because the capillary attraction of the tear film and corneal rigidity cancel each other out at this exact area.
If corneal astigmatism is > 3.00 D, align the 'red' mark on the biprism with the patient's minus-cylinder axis.
Compare IOP between eyes; a difference of >3 mmHg requires clinical correlation.
Always document the time of measurement for glaucoma follow-ups.
